title: Spits, Pumps and Daydreams
summary: About 450 years ago, clever people in Turkey, Spain, France, Italy and England started playing with steam again. One used it to turn a roast on a fire, one used it to pump water out of a mine, and one dreamed of a water fountain driven by fire. None of their machines changed the world yet, but each one was a step on the road.

sections.heading: Steam Wakes Up Again
paragraphs: Imagine walking into a busy workshop in the middle of the 1500s. There are no electric lights and no engines. Every hammer is swung by an arm, every bellows is squeezed by hand, and every heavy load is dragged by people or animals. Yet the air is full of new ideas. Printing presses have been spreading books across Europe for about a hundred years, and old Greek books, including Hero of Alexandria's Pneumatica, are being copied, translated into Latin and Italian, and studied by curious engineers.

For roughly 1,500 years after Hero, steam had mostly been a party trick. Cooks knew that a lid would rattle over boiling water. Metalworkers knew that a sealed pot thrown on a fire could burst with a frightening bang. But almost nobody had tried to make steam do a steady, useful job. Between about 1550 and 1665, that slowly began to change.

In this part of the story, we will travel across a whole continent and beyond. We will visit Istanbul, the glittering capital of the Ottoman Empire, where an astronomer wrote about a spit that turned itself. We will go to Spain, where a soldier who looked after the king's mines received official permission to use a steam device for raising water. We will cross into France and the gardens of German princes with a fountain designer, peek into an Italian book of imaginary machines, and finally stop in London, where a nobleman who had once been locked in the Tower wrote about a 'water-commanding engine'.

These people did not know each other, and most of them could not have read each other's books. They lived in different countries, spoke different languages and followed different religions. But they shared one big question that you met at the end of Part 1: could fire, through water and steam, be made to do work that muscles, wind and rivers usually did?

As you read, notice two things. First, many of these machines were described in books or drawings, but we often do not know how well, or even whether, they worked in real life. A drawing is not the same as a machine that runs every day for years. Second, history books written in Britain have sometimes told the steam story as if it began in England. It did not. Some of the earliest steam ideas of this period came from the Ottoman world and from Spain, and it is only fair to give them their place.

sections.heading: Taqi al-Din and the Self-Turning Spit
paragraphs: Our first stop is with a man named Taqi al-Din Muhammad ibn Ma'ruf. He was born in 1526 in Damascus, in what is now Syria, which was then part of the huge Ottoman Empire. That empire stretched from Hungary to Egypt and from Iraq to Algeria, and its capital, Istanbul (then usually called Constantinople), was one of the largest cities on Earth.

Taqi al-Din was what we would now call a polymath, which means a person who is expert in many subjects. He studied religion and law, but he also loved mathematics, optics (the science of light), astronomy and machines. Over his life he wrote more than ninety books. He worked as a judge and teacher in Egypt and Syria, and in 1571 he became the chief astronomer to the Ottoman sultan.

In 1551, while he was living in Egypt, he finished a book about clever mechanical devices. It was written in Arabic, and its title is usually translated into English as 'The Sublime Methods of Spiritual Machines'. The word 'spiritual' here does not mean ghosts. It was an old way of describing machines that seemed to move by themselves, powered by hidden things like air, water or weights.

One of the machines in the book was a roasting spit. A spit is a long metal rod pushed through a piece of meat so it can be turned slowly over a fire. For thousands of years, somebody had to sit by the hot fire and turn it by hand, hour after hour, so the meat cooked evenly and did not burn on one side. In some places, people even trained small dogs to run inside a wheel to turn the spit.

Taqi al-Din described a way to let the fire do the turning. A closed vessel of water was heated until steam rushed out of a narrow opening. The jet of steam was aimed at vanes, small flat blades arranged around the edge of a wheel. As the steam struck the vanes, it pushed them round, and the wheel turned the spit. The hotter the fire, the faster the steam came out, and the faster the meat would rotate.

Look closely at that idea, because it is important. Hero's aeolipile spun because steam rushed out of the ball itself and pushed it backwards, like a lawn sprinkler. Taqi al-Din's spit worked in a different way: a jet of steam from a fixed nozzle struck the blades of a separate wheel and shoved them along. Engineers today call this an impulse design. Centuries later, in the 1880s, the Swedish engineer Gustaf de Laval would build fast-spinning impulse turbines that used the same basic principle, with far better metal and much more precise blades.

Taqi al-Din's book also described several water-raising machines, including pumps driven by animals and by water wheels, one of them with six cylinders. He later wrote about mechanical clocks and, in the 1570s, ran a new observatory in Istanbul, where he watched the Great Comet of 1577. Sadly, the observatory was torn down in 1580 after political quarrels at the sultan's court. His steam spit, meanwhile, stayed a kitchen curiosity. It saved a little work for a cook, but nobody tried to build it into a giant machine. Still, it is one of the earliest known written descriptions of steam turning a wheel by striking blades.

sections.heading: Jerónimo de Ayanz: A Soldier Who Fought Floods
paragraphs: Our next traveller is a Spanish nobleman with a very long name: Jerónimo de Ayanz y Beaumont. He was born in 1553 in Navarre, in the north of Spain. Like many young noblemen of his time, he became a soldier. He fought in North Africa, in Italy and in the Low Countries (today's Belgium and the Netherlands), and he was known as a brave and very strong man. He was made a knight of the Order of Calatrava, one of Spain's old military orders, and later served as governor of the town of Martos.

In 1587, King Philip II gave Ayanz a very different job. He was made administrator general of the kingdom's mines. Spain at that time ruled a vast empire, and silver from mines in Spain and the Americas helped pay for its armies and palaces. Ayanz was responsible for hundreds of mines, about 550 according to one count, scattered across Spain and its American lands.

That job showed him the same terrible problem that English coal miners faced, which you read about in Part 1. The deeper miners dug, the more groundwater seeped into the tunnels. Water had to be lifted out with buckets, hand pumps and horse-driven machines, and it was slow, costly and exhausting. One of the mines he knew well was at Guadalcanal, in southern Spain, a famous source of silver that suffered badly from flooding.

Ayanz was an inventor at heart. In 1606, King Philip III granted him a 'privilege of invention', a royal document that gave him the sole right to use and profit from his ideas for a set period. In that sense it was like a modern patent. The privilege covered close to fifty different inventions. They included improved windmills, better furnaces, new scientific instruments, a type of pump, and, most importantly for our story, a device that used steam to help raise water. Historians describe it as one of the earliest known patents for any steam device anywhere in the world.

Exactly how his steam water-raiser worked is still studied by historians, because it is known mainly from written descriptions and drawings in the privilege documents rather than from a surviving machine. The basic idea was to use the force of steam from a heated vessel to push water upward, so that a mine could be drained without endless teams of animals. Sources say it was tried at the Guadalcanal mines. How long it worked there, and how much water it really moved, is not well recorded.

Ayanz also loved testing ideas in public. On 2 August 1602, in front of King Philip III and his court, he arranged a demonstration on the Pisuerga River near Valladolid. A man wearing a special diving suit, fed with fresh air through tubes, went under the water and stayed there for about an hour, until the king himself told him he could come up. People watching on the riverbank must have been astonished.

Ayanz died in Madrid in 1613. For a long time afterwards, his name was almost forgotten outside Spain, while English-language books talked mostly about later British engineers. Only in the late 1900s did historians of Spanish engineering carefully study his papers and bring his work back into the light. Today he is often called a pioneer of steam, a reminder that the history of invention can lose people simply because their papers sat unread in an archive.

sections.heading: Salomon de Caus and the Fountain That Ran on Fire
paragraphs: Now let us travel north to France. Salomon de Caus was born in 1576 in Dieppe, a port town on the coast of Normandy. He was a Huguenot, which means a French Protestant, at a time when Protestants and Catholics in France often distrusted and even fought each other. Partly for that reason, de Caus spent much of his life on the move, working wherever a rich patron would hire him.

His speciality was something that sounds like pure fun: gardens full of moving water. Wealthy princes of the early 1600s loved grottoes (artificial caves), splashing fountains, mechanical birds that sang when water flowed through hidden pipes, and statues that seemed to play music. De Caus designed these wonders. He worked in England for the royal family, building a fountain shaped like a rocky mountain, Mount Parnassus, at one of their London palaces. Later he moved to Heidelberg in Germany, where he designed the famous Hortus Palatinus, a huge terraced garden for the ruler of the Palatinate and his English wife, Elizabeth Stuart. Parts of its walls and terraces can still be seen beside Heidelberg Castle today.

To make all those fountains work, de Caus had to think hard about how to move water uphill. In 1615 he published a beautifully illustrated book in French, Les Raisons des forces mouvantes, which means roughly 'The Reasons for Moving Forces'. It was full of pumps, water wheels, organs and garden machines. Among them was a simple but striking experiment with steam.

Here is the idea. Take a strong, hollow metal ball and fill it partly with water. Fit a narrow pipe through the top of the ball, so that the bottom end of the pipe dips almost to the floor of the ball, under the water, while the top end sticks out into the air. Seal everything else tightly. Now put the ball over a fire. As the water heats up, steam collects in the space above the water inside the ball. The steam has nowhere to go, so its pressure rises and presses down on the surface of the water. The only way out is up the pipe, so the water is forced up and spurts out of the top like a fountain.

De Caus did not invent this trick entirely on his own. About fourteen years earlier, in 1601, an Italian scholar named Giambattista della Porta had described a similar way of using steam pressure to raise a column of water. But de Caus's book was widely read, and his drawing became one of the best-known early pictures showing steam pressure pushing water.

There was a big problem with his fountain, though. It could only run once per filling. When the water in the ball was used up, you had to let it cool, open it and refill it. It also needed the ball to be very strong, because steam pressure that can lift a jet of water can also split a weak seam. Metalworkers of the time could not easily make large, safe, pressure-proof vessels.

In the 1800s, some French writers, including the scientist François Arago, claimed that de Caus was the true inventor of the steam engine. That went too far: he never built a working engine that ran on its own. A dramatic story also circulated at that time that he had been locked in a madhouse in Paris for pestering the king's minister about steam power. That tale came from a letter that later turned out to be made up, so it should be treated as a legend. The real de Caus was a respected engineer and garden designer, and he died in Paris in 1626.

sections.heading: Giovanni Branca's Machine on Paper
paragraphs: Our fifth stop is the Italian hill town of Loreto, near the Adriatic Sea. It was, and still is, a famous place of pilgrimage, built around a church called the Holy House. Giovanni Branca, born in 1571, worked there from 1616 as an architect and engineer, looking after the great church buildings.

In 1629 Branca published a book in Rome called Le Machine, which simply means 'The Machines'. It was a collection of illustrated plates showing all kinds of devices: lifting gear, mills, pumps and other contraptions. Picture books of machines like this were popular in Renaissance Europe. They were partly engineering manuals and partly showcases, a bit like a catalogue of amazing ideas.

One plate in Le Machine has become famous in the history of steam. It shows a closed vessel of water sitting on a fire. Steam escapes from a pipe at the top and blows straight at a horizontal wheel fitted with flat vanes around its rim, almost like a small paddle wheel lying on its side. As the steam hits the vanes, the wheel turns. Through a set of gears, its turning motion lifts and drops a pair of heavy pestles, the club-like tools used to pound things in a mortar. Branca suggested that machines like this could grind materials, raise water or saw wood.

If that sounds familiar, it is because it uses the same principle as Taqi al-Din's spit: a jet of steam striking blades. For that reason, Branca's drawing is often shown as an early ancestor of the steam turbine. But there is no evidence that Branca actually built a full working version. Even if he had, it would have been very weak. A loose jet of steam blowing across open air quickly spreads out and slows down, so most of its energy is lost before it ever touches the vanes. Real impulse turbines, built two and a half centuries later, needed carefully shaped nozzles, tight casings and precisely made blades spinning at high speed.

One modern historian of technology, Alex Keller, described many of the machines in books like Branca's as 'armchair inventions', designs that seldom had any working three-dimensional version. That does not make Branca foolish. Drawing an idea is an important first step, and books like his spread ideas to other engineers. But it reminds us that a picture of a machine in a book is not proof that the machine ever ran.

sections.heading: The Marquess and His Water-Commanding Engine
paragraphs: Our final traveller lived through one of the most dangerous periods in English history. Edward Somerset was born in about 1601 into one of the richest Catholic families in England. His family's great home was Raglan Castle in Monmouthshire, on the border between England and Wales. He later became the second Marquess of Worcester.

When the English Civil War broke out in 1642, between supporters of King Charles I and supporters of Parliament, Somerset sided with the king. He raised troops in Wales and was sent on a secret mission to Ireland to try to win soldiers for the royal side. The deal he made there was so generous that the king later disowned it. After the king lost the war, Somerset spent years in exile in France. When he returned to England in the 1650s, he was arrested and held in the Tower of London for a time.

Through all this turmoil, Somerset loved inventing. He kept a skilled mechanic named Caspar Kaltoff (also spelled Kaspar Kalthoff) working with him, and together they built and tested machines. In 1663 he published a little book with a long title, usually known as A Century of Inventions. Here 'century' means 'a hundred', not 'a hundred years': the book lists about one hundred inventions, from secret codes and combination locks to calculating devices and floating gardens.

Most of the entries are only a few lines long, and many are so vague that historians still argue about what he meant. But one entry, about a way of driving water upward by fire, has attracted enormous attention. Somerset called it a 'water-commanding engine'. From his descriptions, it seems that steam from a separate boiler was led into closed vessels of water and its pressure forced the water up a pipe. While one vessel was being emptied by steam, another could be refilled, so the flow could keep going. That idea of separating the boiler from the vessels where the pumping happened was an important step beyond de Caus's single ball.

Somerset claimed big things for his engine. He wrote that it could send water up like a fountain many feet high, around 40 feet (about 12 metres) by his account, and that a small amount of water turned to steam could push up many times its own amount of cold water. Visitors recorded seeing a water-raising machine at his workshop at Vauxhall in London around 1663, and an old account says that, before the Civil War, he tested the idea on the walls of Raglan Castle. In 1663 Parliament even passed an Act allowing him to keep the profits from his water-commanding engine, with a tenth going to the king.

Yet the engine never became a business. Somerset was deep in debt, he struggled to find investors, and some scientists doubted him. Robert Hooke, a brilliant experimenter you will meet in the next part, dismissed the engine as one of the 'perpetual motion fallacies'. Somerset died in 1667. It was said that he wanted a model of his engine buried with him, and in 1861 a group led by the engineer and historian Bennet Woodcroft opened the family vault at Raglan to look for it, but found nothing. Whatever the water-commanding engine really was, it vanished with its inventor.

sections.heading: So Many Ideas, So Few Machines
paragraphs: Let us line up our travellers. In 1551, Taqi al-Din described a steam jet turning a spit. In 1601, della Porta described steam forcing water up a tube. In 1606, Ayanz received a royal privilege that included a steam device for raising water from mines. In 1615, de Caus published his steam fountain. In 1629, Branca drew a steam jet spinning a wheel. In 1663, the Marquess of Worcester described an engine that commanded water with fire. That is more than a century of clever thinking about steam, from Egypt to England.
So why, by the 1660s, was there still not a single steam machine quietly working day after day in a mine or a mill? There were several reasons, and they all fitted together.

First, materials. Steam pressure is powerful, and early metal vessels were often hammered or cast with weak spots and leaky seams soldered with soft metals. If you push too hard, they split or explode. Engineers of the time did not have reliable ways to make big, strong, accurately shaped containers, and they had no good gauges for measuring pressure.

Second, efficiency. Most of these designs wasted huge amounts of heat. A jet of steam blowing on a wheel, or steam pressing directly on cold water, loses heat and energy very quickly. To pump a meaningful amount of water, you would have needed a great deal of fuel, and in many places wood and coal were expensive.

Third, nobody yet understood the science. People did not know what steam really was, how air pressure worked, or why water behaved as it did when heated and cooled. Without that knowledge, every improvement was guesswork. Building a better machine was a bit like trying to fix a bicycle in the dark.

Fourth, there was not always a clear customer who desperately needed the machine and could pay for it. Garden fountains and turning spits were nice to have, but they did not justify building expensive, dangerous equipment. That would change once mines grew deeper and their owners grew desperate, as you will see in Part 5.

It is also worth noticing who was doing this thinking: an Ottoman astronomer, a Spanish soldier and mine official, a French Protestant garden designer, an Italian church architect and an English Catholic nobleman. Invention was not the property of one country. Ideas were scattered all across the world, and many people built small pieces of the puzzle without ever seeing the whole picture.

And here is the surprise. When the first truly practical steam engines finally appeared, about forty to fifty years after Worcester's book, they did not mainly use steam to push. The real breakthrough came from something stranger: the discovery that the empty space called a vacuum is real, and that the invisible air around us is heavy enough to press with enormous force. To understand that discovery, we need to visit a glassblower's tube full of shining mercury, a mountain in France, and a town where teams of horses tried and failed to pull two metal bowls apart. That is the story of Part 4.

deepDive: Who invented the steam engine? The honest answer is that there was no single moment and no single inventor, and the period from 1550 to 1665 shows why the question is slippery. Historians usually separate four stages: a written idea, a drawing, a working model and a machine that runs reliably for paying customers. Taqi al-Din (1551) and Branca (1629) give us the first two stages for the steam jet striking vanes, which is the principle of the impulse turbine. Della Porta (1601) and de Caus (1615) describe steam pressure forcing water up a pipe, the principle behind the 'pressure' half of Thomas Savery's later pump. Ayanz (1606) and Worcester (1663) seem to have gone further, toward working water-raisers, but surviving evidence is thin: for Ayanz it is mainly privilege documents and drawings, and for Worcester it is a short, deliberately mysterious book, a few visitors' reports and an Act of Parliament. Priority claims have also been shaped by national pride. In the 1800s, French writers championed de Caus, British books celebrated Worcester and Savery, and Spanish historians later rediscovered Ayanz. Even older claims exist: a story says a Spanish sea captain, Blasco de Garay, showed a steam-driven ship to Emperor Charles V in 1543, but the evidence is doubtful and most historians reject it. Why did none of these designs take off? Look at the physics. A free steam jet in open air loses most of its kinetic energy to turbulence before reaching the vanes, so Branca-type wheels deliver only a tiny fraction of the fuel's energy as useful work. Pressure-displacement devices like de Caus's ball heat the water they are pushing, wasting heat, and they demand vessels that can safely hold pressure, which was hard with 1600s metalworking. The missing ingredient was not cleverness but understanding: until scientists explained atmospheric pressure and the vacuum in the 1640s to 1690s, inventors lacked a reliable model of what steam and air were actually doing.
funFact: In 1602, a diver wearing an air-supplied suit designed by Jerónimo de Ayanz stayed under the Pisuerga River for about an hour, until King Philip III himself told him to come up.
